props.title: The Acid House

sections.content: The Acid House represents one of the boldest adaptations of Irvine Welsh's provocative writing, following the success of Trainspotting (1996). Director Paul McGuigan crafts three interconnected stories that plunge into Edinburgh's gritty underbelly, mixing surreal black comedy with social commentary. Like Welsh's other adaptations, including Filth (2013), the film employs shocking imagery and thick Scottish dialects to capture the author's raw literary style. The anthology format allows exploration of different tones, from dark comedy to psychological horror.

sections.content: The film's experimental nature connects it to other British films pushing boundaries in the late 1990s. Twin Town (1997) shared similar themes of working-class dysfunction, while Shopping (1994) captured youth rebellion through a darker lens. The surreal elements, particularly in the story where a man switches consciousness with a baby, echo the hallucinatory sequences of Fear and Loathing in Las Vegas (1998) released the same year.

The film's anthology structure allows examination of different aspects of Scottish working-class life, similar to how Sweet Sixteen (2002) and Red Road (2006) would later explore Glasgow's social issues. The raw performances and unflinching approach to controversial subject matter established a template for later British films like Dead Man's Shoes (2004) and This Is England (2006). sections.content: The Acid House helped cement the growing confidence of Scottish cinema in the late 1990s, alongside films like Ratcatcher (1999) and Orphans (1998). Its mix of social realism and surreal elements influenced later works like Under the Skin (2013) and You Were Never Really Here (2017), showing how Scottish cinema could balance artistic ambition with grounded storytelling.
